title: An eccentric planet on WASP-105 B requires a close stellar passage in a quadrupole excitation model
abstract: We test whether the wide stellar orbit can drive the eccentricity needed for the two-day WASP-105 signal to come from its faint M-dwarf companion. We combine standard quadrupole secular energy conservation, general relativity, and a static planetary tide with exact projected Kepler orbit geometry. Excitation from a circular orbit to eccentricity 0.5 requires stellar pericentre below 0.0825 AU at projected separation 72 AU, or below 0.0646 AU at 92 AU, for a 10-Earth-mass, 3.9-Earth-radius planet with Love number 0.3. All 27 tested planet parameter choices require pericentre below 8.30 planet semimajor axes. None meets an explicit ten-axis hierarchy floor. We also derive a necessary upper bound on the instantaneous stellar position-angle rate. Its largest value in the parameter grid is 0.049 degrees per year. This gives a test with calibrated relative astrometry without a full binary orbit. Numerical integrations check the secular calculation, and synthetic Kepler states check the projection inequalities. The result limits one excitation route. It does not identify the transit host, confirm the planet, establish a universal stability floor, or cover octupole effects, close passages, primordial eccentricity, or other perturbers. No new telescope data are used. Original code, aggregate inputs, source hashes, simulated results, and reproduction instructions are included.

display.caption: Necessary pericentre and instantaneous position-angle-rate bounds for a nearly circular initial planet on WASP-105 B. Solid curves include GR and the nominal static tide. The finite PA difference is illustrative and has no calibrated error here.

citations.reason: Rounded aggregate host and planet parameters. We replace a circular wide-orbit torque estimate with necessary bounds over unknown bound stellar Kepler orbits in a specified secular model.
Discovery of the two-day candidate that motivates this conditional host test.
